## ABSTRACT

The United Nations is the arena for a renewed push to regulate transnational corporations (TNCs) and their supply chains. This article analyses the ongoing efforts of a multilateral organization to strengthen the human rights legal framework, especially the design choices posed by the treaty negotiations as well as the role of the UN Human Rights Council in the broader regulatory ecosystem around TNCs. Is there complementarity or conflict among on-going initiatives to regulate TNCs? Is there continuity or fracture in the successive waves of UN attempts to legalize TNC responsibilities? The analytical lenses are human rights due diligence with an emphasis on root causes, which is a gateway for exploring more systemic interventions. Thus, deeper causes of harm identifiable in global supply chains operations are identified and systematically compared to see how public and private norm-setters take them into account or downplay them. For this purpose, the article draws on treaty drafts and reports from the UN Intergovernmental Working Group and materials from four other areas: responsible business conduct, due diligence laws, the UN Guiding Principles, and the UN’s earlier efforts at TNC regulation.

## 1. Introduction

As the broadest multilateral organization with a human rights mandate, the UN has a unique part to play in advancing corporate and state accountability. It also has five decades experience wrestling with the ‘TNC problem’ and attempting to design normative standards and regulatory frameworks. Footnote 1 This article explores the current work of the Human Rights Council in its attempt to set legal standards on corporate human rights responsibilities. Several questions guide this analysis. Does this treaty making process mark continuity or fracture with previous TNC-related efforts of the UN: the 1970s Code, the 2000s Norms, and the 2010s Guiding Principles? Do the treaty drafts suggest compatibility or divergence with legalization models emerging outside the UN, such as mandatory due diligence instruments adopted or anticipated in the European Union? Is the UN able to account and adapt to a shifting global context? Footnote 2 Does the Council risk internal incoherence and mixed messages on business and human rights (BHR) when the Guiding Principles and the draft treaty are compared? Has the UN in the last 20 years betrayed its ideals enshrined in the UN Charter and does it have now a chance to redeem itself? Footnote 3 Judging by Intergovernmental Working Group’s (IGWG) deliberations, will the Council – the focal point on human rights in the UN system – facilitate innovation towards a BHR regime grounded in international law or risk irrelevance as others, within Footnote 4 and outside UN system, Footnote 5 might assume leading roles?

This article examines the treaty design emerging from the IGWG process as well as the role of the UN in the broader, accelerating process of legalization in BHR. The article concentrates on the core concept in the Guiding Principles – human rights due diligence – to analyze if some of its key parameters are reflected in the treaty drafts and IGWG deliberations in order to gauge whether and how the UN treaty aligns with and facilitates other on-going processes of legalization in BHR outside the UN. One such due diligence parameter relates to root cause of human rights violations. Therefore this analysis looks into what root causes of business misconduct the draft treaty seems to recognize or ignore, and how they affect the content, ratification and implementation on the treaty. As to the broader legalization process, there is a changed regulatory context affecting the UN treaty deliberations and the role the UN might play in a broader regulatory ecosystem: public regulations (of some states that adopted or ponder on mandating due diligence) that coexist and interact with private governance (responsible business conduct as evidenced by business policies and multistakeholder initiatives).

The article draws on UN materials up to the 2020 Intergovernmental Group session. The analysis is structured in the following sections: human rights due diligence with its root cause parameter (section 3), IGWG’s deliberations (section 4), business policy in the area of purchasing practices (section 5), national due diligence regulations (section 6), relation to previous unsuccessful UN attempt to regulate TNCs (section 7), and implications for the content of the treaty and UN’s role in the wider BHR ecosystem (section 8).

## 2. Institutional context and summary of current UN negotiations

The United Nations is once again the arena for a push to regulate transnational corporations (TNCs) and their value chains. The UN has been at this job for close to 50 years starting with the 1970s when developing countries pushed for a Code on TNCs and a New International Economic Order (NIEO). Footnote 6 That Code was shelved in 1992 and so was the next attempt, the Draft Norms, Footnote 7 in 2004. The third attempt to adopt an instrument on corporate responsibilities succeeded in 2011 when states in the Human Rights Council (‘Council’) unanimously endorsed the Guiding Principles on business and human rights (‘Guiding Principles’ or UNGPs). Footnote 8 

Building on the momentum created this soft law instrument, but also responding to its inherent limitations in terms of remediation for victims and legal liability of companies, the Council signaled in 2014 the start of a treaty making process. So with the endorsement of a large coalition of civil society groups, an Intergovernmental Working Group (‘Intergovernmental Group’ or IGWG) was tasked to ‘elaborate an international legally binding instrument to regulate the activities of transnational corporations’. Footnote 9 By 2021 a treaty is taking shape through three successive drafts being discussed in annual IGWG sessions. Footnote 10 

The Human Rights Council, the UN’s primary human rights body made up of 47 member states, Footnote 11 has been an important loci for developing a normative framework for MNEs since the 1990s, at that time the Human Rights Commission. Before the 1990s, normative frameworks for TNCs were developed by the UN Center on Transnational Corporations Footnote 12 as well as specialized UN agencies such as the ILO. Footnote 13 The UN Secretary General commenced an innovative though controversial business initiative – the UN Global Compact – in 2000. After the adoption of the Guiding Principles, in 2011 the Council set up an expert Working Group tasked with promoting the Principles Footnote 14 and this group coexists now with the political Intergovernmental Working Group tasked with developing a treaty. Institutionally, the former group informs and participates in the latter’s deliberations.

The Intergovernmental Working Group meets annually for sessions of five days and has been chaired by Ecuador since the beginning. It is open for participation to all Member States, to International Organizations and NGOs having consultative status. From within the UN, ‘special procedures’ such as the Working Group on business and human rights, also participate. Furthermore, other experts are invited to panel discussions in line with the Council’s resolution that affirmed the importance of independent expertise and advice. Footnote 15 Attendance fluctuates from year to year and the reports from each session identify the participants from all these groups. Irrespective the deep disagreements around the entire treaty initiative, the Chair has been commended for the participatory way in which deliberations proceed.

Within the UN system, there is also the UNCTAD framework Footnote 16 and its work on investment and trade that regularly highlights the various societal impacts and changing patterns of transnational flows of goods, services and capital. Footnote 17 Also related to sustainability, the UN Agenda 2030 emphasises the role of the private sector in achieving the sustainable development goals and respecting human rights in line with the Guiding Principles. Footnote 18 This constellation of UN agencies and normative frameworks led some observers to wonder whether the UN normative efforts regarding business and human rights have become ‘fractured and dissipated’. Footnote 19 

Noteworthy, the Guiding Principles marked a demonstrable process of convergence in soft law within and outside the UN on the corporate responsibility to respect human rights. Footnote 20 Thus within the Council system, the special procedures and treaty bodies began to incorporate immediately and systematically the Principles in their work. Footnote 21 The treaty process underway could further consolidate such convergence of expectations and widespread use of the Principles. In terms of treaty design, what is emerging from the Intergovernmental Group’s deliberations points to continuity in international human rights law. Thus, the Group put aside early on some initial proposals to create direct obligations on TNCs. Similarly, a stronger oversight machinery – a court or another mechanism to hold states (or businesses) answerable – is not in the cards either. Instead, the drafts create instant familiarity as the proposed drafts use the common template of states’ obligations to protect rights and their obligations to report to the UN. Footnote 22 

The treaty process has been contentious since its inception in 2014. Actually, the resolution setting up the IGWG mandate was duplicated by another resolution focused on the further implementation of the UNGPs. Footnote 23 Furthermore, industrialised states received frostily the treaty initiative, with the US boycotting and the EU merely observing the deliberations. This article examines the ramification of this design and treaty-making effort in the broader context. As many commentators recognise, the treaty is not the silver bullet regulatory solution to corporate unaccountability. Therefore it is important for an analysis of the treaty to account for developments in corporate self-regulation and other legalization occurring outside the multilateral UN context. In the same time, the UN has a unique role to play and the proposed treaty is part of a regulatory ecosystem of multilevel governance, it is shaped by it and it has a crucial role in facilitating the further development of this ecosystem.
